articles.title_orig: The Rise and Rise of Alice Huang
articles.title_zh: The Rise and Rise of Alice Huang
articles.content_orig:
In 2019 Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, made $145 million from the sale of an online gaming group that three years earlier had annual revenues of just $36,000.
According to a securities filing , Ms Huang’s sale of her British Virgin Islands-based holding company, Osmanthus Vale Holdings Limited, came shortly after its revenues had soared 1,000 fold to $36 million in 2018. The transaction was also the catalyst for a dramatic career shift for Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, who by 2023 had risen to become managing director of a major data-center operator and Nvidia partner, Singapore-based Megaspeed.
The company that purchased Osmanthus from Huang was 7Road Holdings, a video game developer based in Shenzhen and listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.
In 2021, 7Road entered the cloud computing industry, just before the release of ChatGPT created a boom in such stocks. But when the Biden administration imposed export controls on China in October 2022, the company could no longer buy the most advanced AI chips from the likes of Nvidia.
7Road decided to spin off its Singapore subsidiary, which could buy America’s best AI chips. That subsidiary, 7Road International PTE, was sold to a BVI-registered company associated with Ms Huang and renamed Megaspeed.
Megaspeed went on to buy billions of dollars worth of servers containing advanced Nvidia AI chips, and is the subject of U.S. and Singapore government investigations into whether it smuggled chips to China.
As of November 11, Nvidia continues to list Megaspeed as an official partner on its website.
The New York Times and Financial Times were the first to report, respectively, that U.S. officials suspected Ms Huang worked for China’s state security ministry and had an affair with Jensen Huang. China’s foreign ministry denied that Ms Huang worked for the MSS.
Jensen Huang told Bloomberg there was nothing improper about his relationship with Ms Huang.
The Nvidia founder subsequently admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, but did not admit to an affair with Ms Huang.
President Donald Trump said that, in a phone call with Jensen Huang, the Nvidia founder told him he was unaware of any connections Ms Huang might have to China’s intelligence service. The scandal will hang over the president’s Asia trip next week to attend summits in the Philippines and China.
The 7Road deal was just one of many that would propel Ms Huang into the world of AI data centers.
She started her career as a news reporter for state television before moving into finance, according to her bio at an investment firm where she later worked. She eventually became the executive director of the firm, Shanghai Hexi Investment Fund, according to the Asset Management Association of China, a regulatory body.
Funds associated with Hexi invested alongside the Zhejiang Century Huatong Group, a maker of internet video games, as it entered the cloud computing business.
Between 2021 and 2022, Ms Huang served as a director of Shanghai Longjing Information Technology, according to corporate records accessed through WireScreen . The company was founded in December 2020 as a data-center focused subsidiary of Huatong. That same month, Huatong acquired a 10 percent stake in 7Road, securities filings show.
Seducing foreign executives is a common tactic used by China’s Ministry of State Security, especially on their visits to China, says Randal Phillips , a former CIA Beijing station chief. “The lion’s share of [MSS] resources were devoted to [compromising] private sector interests,” he adds.
WireScreen records show that Shanghai Longjing’s legal representative is Gu Jiong, who worked with Ms Huang at Shanghai Hexi Investment Fund, according to the fund’s website. Gu was also the legal representative of Hangzhou Shengfeng Network Technology, a Chinese video games company that Alice Huang sold to 7Road in 2019. Gu could not be reached for comment.
In 2023, the Shanghai municipal government announced that Shanghai Longjing would build a data center with 6,000 AI server racks at a larger complex where Tencent is a major tenant.
Tencent rents rack space from Shanghai Longjing that it fills with its own chips, according to people close to Tencent. When it is finished, the complex will provide 10 times as much computing power as the world’s largest supercomputer, according to Shanghai’s Songjiang district government .
A Tencent spokesperson said the company has never had a stake in, or operated, the complex.
It is not clear if Ms Huang held an operational role at Shanghai Longjing. She could not be reached for comment and the firm did not respond to a request for comment.
Huatong and 7Road did not respond to requests for comment.
Ms Huang’s involvement in several financing deals raises questions of whether she was a corporate fixer. Desmond Shum , whose ex-wife Duan Weihong held billions of dollars in shares of insurance company Ping An on behalf of the family of former Chinese premier Wen Jiabao, said Huang appeared to be a “white glove” — an investor whose name appears on documents on behalf of others.
In 2025, the China Securities Regulatory Commission fined Kang Wei, the founder of Shanghai Hexi, $375,000 for failing to make proper disclosures after he used complex investment vehicles to acquire an electronics company.
Osmanthus, Ms Huang’s video-game investment vehicle, had been incorporated in the British Virgin Islands less than two months before 7Road bought it, according to securities filings . Shanghai Hexi was the firm’s “ultimate holding company.”
Osmanthus’ biggest operating subsidiary was Hangzhou Shengfeng. According to a corporate filing , a Hexi-backed fund purchased Hangzhou Shengfeng from Century Huatong in 2017 for 500 million yuan (around $75 million). In 2019 the fund transferred Hangzhou Shengfeng to newly formed offshore entities, which were consolidated under Osmanthus, securities filings show.
That acquisition could explain the exponential jump in Osmanthus’ revenues, from $36,000 in 2016 to $36 million in 2018.
It is not clear how Ms Huang came to own 100 percent of Osmanthus.
“A woman whose documented career centered on corporate restructuring, leveraged acquisitions, and offshore holding companies suddenly emerged as the public face of [Megaspeed,] a multibillion-dollar AI infrastructure business,” Shum wrote on Substack.
Alice Huang served as Megaspeed’s managing director from March to November of 2023, according to corporate records. That November Megaspeed’s shares were transferred to another company, Swiftdata Pte, which had been incorporated just weeks earlier. By the end of 2024, Megaspeed’s assets had jumped to $3 billion, from just $33 million the year prior. The sole current director of Swiftdata is Tan Yong Pong, a Singaporean citizen, corporate records show.
Megaspeed said on Monday that there is “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities.” The company did not respond to a request for comment.
A spokesperson for the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which enforces export controls, declined to comment when asked if it is considering taking any measures targeting Megaspeed.
Nvidia has long lobbied for weakening the export controls that prevent it from selling AI chips to China. President Trump loosened controls on Nvidia’s H200 chip last year.
Nvidia initially said Jensen Huang’s relationship with Ms Huang was “not unusual.” On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced that it will open an inquiry into whether Jensen Huang was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.” Its share price has dropped around 10 percent over the past five days.
The FBI is also looking into a matter related to Jensen Huang, Trump said at a press conference on Monday, without offering specifics.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq gains more than 1% as CoreWeave spike revitalizes AI trade: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq gains more than 1% as CoreWeave spike revitalizes AI trade: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
CoreWeave shares jumped 24.71% Wednesday for its best day since April 2025 after the neocloud posted quarterly earnings that beat estimates and raised its guidance for the year.
"Demand for the infrastructure is and remains overwhelming." CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Wednesday.
"I think I said that we are 10x oversubscribed to the existing capacity that we have left in 2027, and we are multiples ... oversubscribed on the capacity we have out in 2028," he said.
Neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN have come under scrutiny this month as investors assessed the sustainability of the AI trade. CoreWeave, in particular, sparked alarm when spreads on its CDS widened past 11% , generally viewed as a distress level, as investors have to pay up for protection against default. With the price of its high-yield debt climbing, CoreWeave highlighted additional routes to finance its data center build-out with less alarming yields, quelling investor concerns for the time being.
"Our asset level debt has basically been rock solid through this entire thing," Intrator told CNBC. "There is an enormous demand for that product. We're about to launch another asset-level debt in the next week or two that has already been rated high investment grade." Intrator added that he expects it "will be underwritten in the market at 7% to 7.5% interest," which will bring down the average weighted cost of capital for the company.
The three months to Sept. 30 marked a "breakout quarter" for CoreWeave, Intrator said on the conference call, adding that growth was supported by multiple sources of funding, including financing backed by customer contracts and around $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits.
Revenue jumped 168% to $3.7 billion in the third quarter, the company said in a Tuesday statement .
Other neclouds also rose on CoreWeave's strong results, with Nebius rising 15.44%, Applied Digital 7.37% and Iren 5.63% Wednesday.
Despite fears that a "blue wave" in last week's midterm elections could restrict data center capacity, Intrator reiterated that data center growth looks poised to continue as expected for CoreWeave.
"We don't see any impact on our ability to deliver the data centers within the U.S. that are required for us to deliver on our backlog," Intrator told CNBC on Wednesday. "In Texas, Governor-elect [Gina Hinojosa], said that facilities that are permitted and under construction will continue, and we've been really, really thoughtful about the broad distribution."
CoreWeave expects $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion in adjusted operating income on $13 billion to $13.3 billion in revenue. Analysts surveyed by Visible Alpha were looking for $1.07 billion in adjusted operating income, and analysts polled by LSEG had expected $12.86 billion in 2026 revenue.
The neocloud has done well to allay concerns about financing by moving away from unsecured bond financing, Zacks Chief Equity Strategist John Blank told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe."
"It might be the bottom for CoreWeave," Blank said Wednesday. "But the shares are so beaten up, you have to believe at this point there's more value on the upside than the down."
— CNBC's Jordan Novet and Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: How Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got entangled in a China chip and spy scandal
articles.content_orig:

A relationship between the high-profile CEO of Nvidia Jensen Huang and a businesswoman suspected of spying for Beijing has sent shockwaves through political and technology circles.
Alice Huang , who worked in Chinese finance before moving into tech with a leadership position at a Singapore data center firm, reportedly maintained a close relationship with the head of the California company whose chips power advanced artificial intelligence systems.
Reporting over the past month by the New York Times revealed that top policymakers received a memo outlining intelligence that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an operative for China’s Ministry of State Security. The intelligence indicated she had been recruited to sway Nvidia into making its top-tier microchips more accessible within China.
A widely shared 2024 photograph, uploaded to LinkedIn by software firm NetThunder, captures Jensen Huang and others holding drinks in Taipei, with Alice Huang seated behind him, seemingly watching him speak.
The precise duration of the affair and the timing of its conclusion remain unknown and Alice Huang couldn’t be reached for comment.
Very little publicly available information exists regarding Alice Huang. She worked as a Chinese finance executive before transitioning into the artificial intelligence, data center, and computer chip sectors.
In 2023, Huang became a director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a firm that characterizes itself as an "NVIDIA cloud partner." The business faced scrutiny from the U.S. last year over allegations of circumventing U.S. export restrictions and routing significant quantities of advanced Nvidia chips to users in China.
Corporate registration records show Megaspeed was originally incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International, functioning as an overseas spin-off for a Chinese video game developer.
Filings reveal that the business rebranded as Megaspeed International in March 2023, with all shares being transferred to Huang Le Limited, an entity registered in the British Virgin Islands.
That same month, research from C4ADS, a Washington-based non-profit focused on global security, showed that Alice Huang became the controlling shareholder of Megaspeed.
However, by November 2023, Huang was no longer listed as a director at Megaspeed, and her full shareholding was transferred to Tan Yong Pong, a Singaporean businessman who is also known as James Tan.
While public documents indicate Alice Huang departed Megaspeed, short seller Culper Research published a report in May citing a company employee who stated Huang was "actually still our boss" and remained involved in daily operations.
Before her involvement with Megaspeed, Alice Huang held senior executive positions at Chinese firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Co. from around 2015 to 2017, according to records from Chinese private equity database Simuwang and social media posts.
According to social media posts by Hexi, her roles there included deputy general manager, executive director, and member of the investment committee, among potential other responsibilities.
Hexi's founder Kang Wei, whose name appeared alongside Alice Huang on certain records, was fined 400,000 yuan ($60,000) by China's securities regulator in 2018 over financial misconduct, while Hexi itself received a fine of 17.7 million yuan ($2.7 million).
Prior to that, Alice Huang worked within HSBC’s private banking division in Hong Kong and at CITIC Securities, a Chinese investment bank.
Neither HSBC nor CITIC immediately responded to requests for comment regarding her employment history.
When questioned by lawmakers and reporters this week about Megaspeed and Alice Huang, Taiwan’s Interior Minister Liu Shyh-fang stated that authorities, including national security officials, are "actively" investigating the matter, adding that Huang would be prevented from returning to Taiwan.
Beijing has denied allegations that Alice Huang was working as a Chinese operative. The Foreign Ministry stated this week that the "Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China."
With the emergence of the latest scandal, Singapore-based AI computing company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a senior executive, is once again in the spotlight.
Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, was originally incorporated in 2015 before changing its name to Megaspeed International in 2023. Nvidia lists Megaspeed as a partner on its website, while Megaspeed says on its website it's “a core business partner of NVIDIA’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region.”
It was the overseas gaming arm of Shenzhen-based developer 7Road Holdings Ltd.
Late last year, Megaspeed denied accusations following reports that it was routing Nvidia chips to China, saying in a statement on its website that “there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities.”
Singapore’s government said in late October, after fresh reports that Alice Huang was accused of being a Chinese intelligence source, that authorities were investigating Megaspeed and that Singapore “does not condone businesses” circumventing or violating other countries’ export controls. However, it said, there were no investigations conducted in respect to Alice Huang.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Maeve Cullinan is a reporter for The Telegraph’s Global Health Security desk. She covers issues including disease outbreaks, conflict, global development, humanitarian crises, and sexual violence and has reported from Africa and Asia. She was named on the Press 30 under 30 list in 2025.
Far more US farm workers are infected with bird flu than officially reported, with some suffering “very severe” symptoms, according to the country’s largest farming union.
H5N1 is currently spreading rapidly across US cattle farms in dozens of US states.
Officially, just three people have been diagnosed with the virus in the past month, all following close contact with infected cows.
In total, 73 people in the US have been officially been recorded as infected with H5N1 since 2024, mostly dairy farm workers. Three have died.
But United Farm Unions (UFU), which represents thousands of workers across the US, said it was aware of many more farmers experiencing symptoms consistent with H5N1 who had not been tested.
“We have now connected with a number of workers and have confirmed that more workers are sick with avian flu symptoms who have not been tested,” the UFU wrote on X.
Symptoms range from “very mild to very severe”, the post added, including mild upper respiratory infections and conjunctivitis to severe flu-like symptoms, bone pain, persistent coughing and high fever.
The ongoing outbreak is worrying disease experts.
“H5N1 is not a virus to be casual about- or to let spread unchecked, given every mutation is like the virus buying a lottery ticket to acquire human-to-human transmission,” said Dr Devi Sridhar, a public health researcher at the University of Edinburgh.
Referring to the statement by the UFU, Professor Francois Balloux, director of the UCL Genetics Institute, added: “The most puzzling aspect to me is not even the incompetence and paralysis of the authorities but the resignation and fatalism. It feels like reading some chronicle by a mediaeval peasant.”
Of the roughly 1,000 people infected with H5N1 since the virus was first identified in the late 1990s, almost half have died. However, most historical cases have resulted from contact with wild birds, while the strain circulating in cattle, known as genotype B.12, is thought to cause much milder illness.
Concerns have nevertheless grown after an unidentified farm worker in Washington state died in late October from the cattle-derived H5N1 strain, raising questions about whether the virus may have mutated.
The Trump administration has been heavily criticised for allowing bird flu to run rampant through America’s wild and domestic animals, putting people at risk.
Deep cuts to the federal agencies responsible for managing human and animal health, the US Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and the Department of Agriculture (USDA), have resulted in the scaling down of surveillance and testing programmes amongst both livestock and farm workers.
Every infection, animal or human, raises the chance the virus could mutate and eventually gain the ability to spread between people – something which experts have long warned could trigger the next pandemic.
As flu season begins, experts are concerned a dairy worker infected with ordinary seasonal flu could catch H5N1 at the same time, and the two viruses could mix to create a new, more dangerous strain that could spread between people – a phenomenon known as “reassortment.”
“It is clear that workers are not being informed of the risks of handling sick cattle and infected milk. They are being given no information on flu shots or avian flu testing,” the UFU said.
Estimates suggest that over half of the 150,000-strong dairy workforce in the US are immigrant or undocumented workers, driven in part by high demand for intensive year-round labour and a lack of domestic applicants.
Many are reportedly worried about coming forward for testing over fears they will come into contact with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the federal agency emboldened under Trump, which has been tasked with deporting one million immigrants every year.
Yakima Valley, the region of Washington State where the three recent H5N1 cases have been reported and where the virus is spreading through dozens of dairy herds, is in the midst of an ICE crackdown.
The area, which is home to a large community of Hispanic people, saw a nearly three-fold increase in ICE arrests from January to July this year compared to the year before, with 522 people arrested in the seven months.
“Given the current and ongoing ICE surge in the Yakima Valley, many or most of the workers are understandably reluctant to proactively engage with public agencies,” UFU said.
“Protecting dairy workers protects everyone. The front line of this risk, the human firewall, are the workers in the dairies,” the post concluded.
Britain continues to be plagued by an H5N1 outbreak, mostly amongst farmed poultry. From Friday, November 13, all farmed birds in the UK will be subject to a mandatory ‘flockdown ’- where they are kept inside for an indefinite period - to try and prevent the virus spreading between farms.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Iran vows not to part with "single particle of enriched nuclear material" as standoff continues
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Iran vows not to part with "single particle of enriched nuclear material" as standoff continues
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the latest U.S. official to be threatened or targeted by Iran, but he is far from the first.
The Iranian regime has been implicated in various plots to target top U.S. officials since 2020, when President Trump ordered the killing of Iranian general Qassem Soleimani .
Threats against Americans have ramped up since the start of the war with Iran. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned in October that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" abroad, with plots to kill Americans reaching "advanced stages" in the Middle East and other countries.
U.S. households are expected to face higher costs this winter to warm their homes, especially those depending on heating oil, according to a new forecast.
Winter heating costs are expected to average $1,002 for all fuels for the season, up 7.1% from last winter, according to projections released this week from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association.
But a much sharper increase will hit properties reliant on home heating oil , a particularly popular source in the Northeast for which prices have swelled due to the Iran war.
Those households will pay $2,977 this winter, up 70.2% from last year.
The association pointed to declines in home heating prices in recent weeks, but "families should not assume that prices will continue to fall," said executive director Mark Wolfe.
Nationwide, more than 4 million households use heating oil as their primary fuel source, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, and of those, 82% are concentrated in the Northeast.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called for dialogue and restraint to ease regional tensions during a meeting Wednesday with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, according to Sharif's office.
Sharif expressed deep concern over the prolonged conflict as the two spoke on the sidelines of the United Nations climate summit in Turkey, his office said. The prime minister stressed the need to build on an interim deal reached between the U.S. and Iran in June.
In August, Pezeshkian described the deal as the best way for Iran to move on from a situation that he described as "neither war nor peace."
President Trump said Wednesday the U.S. has already won the war against Iran, but when the conflict will end is a different question.
"America did not start a war with Iran," he said at a Veterans Day event at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia. "Iran has been waging war on America since 1979. This should have been taken care of a long time ago."
"Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back," he continued. "All of us fought back. We fought back. And we seriously fought back. And we won. Just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory. It's going to be total. It'll take them 25 years to rebuild back what we have destroyed, and hopefully we won't have to destroy any more of that country."
The president reminded Americans that the Korean War lasted much longer and cost more lives, as did the Vietnam War and the Iraq War.
As he has been saying for months, Mr. Trump said the conflict will be over soon.
Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened to strike U.S. bases beyond the Middle East, including in Europe, if they are used for attacks against the Islamic Republic.
"If American aircraft take off from an American military base, even one located in a European country or some other distant region, to bomb Iran, we will strike those bases as well," Rezaei told Lebanon-based Al Mayadeen TV in an interview broadcast Wednesday.
In a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday, President Trump said he does not currently see "any reason" to escalate the war.
Rezaei also said that Iran's response to renewed U.S. attacks would "target America's more distant military installations — including the ones we have not yet attacked," without specifying.
"We may even strike certain islands that they assume are beyond the reach of our missiles," he added during the interview, which was conducted in Tehran.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday that it shot down three cruise missiles fired at Riyadh, which has been targeted for weeks by the Iran-backed group.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed 3 cruise missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward the Riyadh area," coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki posted on social media.
The latest incident comes after the Houthis damaged a skyscraper belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco in the capital's gleaming financial district on Sunday.
Riyadh's international airport has also been targeted repeatedly, with deadly attacks forcing it to close for two weeks last month.
Saudi Arabia formed an international coalition to fight the Houthis in 2015, after the group's takeover of Yemen's capital Sanaa.
After years of an uneasy truce, the conflict reignited in July.
Iran's Defense Ministry on Wednesday rejected Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's latest blustery assessment of Tehran's military capacities, calling his depiction a fabrication and insisting Iranian armed forces still had weapons stockpiled.
Iran's weapons stockpile "far exceeds the deceptive figures fabricated by Trump and the defeated Pete," a ministry spokesperson said, adding that the country had made use of "strategic production and upgraded technologies."
Hegseth told reporters Tuesday that during 40 days of combat, the U.S. had struck 13,000 targets, destroying, he said, more than 80% of Iran's nuclear industrial base.
"Their navy sunk, their air force grounded, their defense industrial base gone," Hegseth said.
Iranian officials claimed a month ago that the country's weapons production capacity had increased by 250% since the war began, with help from Russia and China.
Neither side has offered evidence to prove their claims, and neither the U.S. nor Iran have launched large-scale strikes since the summer. Both claim to have won the war, but despite Hegseth's assertion on Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz is under U.S. control, Iran continues attacking vessels daily in and near the waterway.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a military base following a series of Iranian threats against his life.
"The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran's economy," a Treasury Department spokesperson said.
A source familiar with the situation pointed to a Wall Street Journal story as the impetus for the move.
"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety," the person told CBS News.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accused the U.S. on Wednesday of threatening to attack his country with America's largest non-nuclear weapon — the "mother of all bombs" — while claiming to seek a diplomatic resolution to the war.
In a post on X , Pezeshkian criticized the U.S. for what he called an effort to "pursue diplomacy through threats."
"No contradiction but a disgrace. Who threatens global peace and security?" he wrote.
CBS News reported in October that the White House and Pentagon had prepared plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB — an acronym that has earned it the nickname used by Pezeshkian —   to hit military sites in Iran if President Trump were to give the order, according to sources familiar with the matter.

articles.title_orig: Why is gasoline suddenly under $4 a gallon?
articles.title_zh: Why is gasoline suddenly under $4 a gallon?
articles.content_orig:
AUSTIN, TEXAS - NOVEMBER 26: A gas pump is seen in a vehicle on November 26, 2025 in Austin, Texas. Brandon Bell/Getty Images hide caption
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Drivers are starting to see some relief from high fuel prices. For the first time in months, the average price of a gallon of gasoline has dipped below $4, according to AAA .
The price crossed below the $4 threshold on Tuesday, and is currently down to a national average of $3.94 for a gallon of regular. Prices have dipped about 40 cents over the past month, with much of that decline happening in the past two weeks.
"Many will assume the election had something to do with it, but that's a myth," Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, wrote in his industry newsletter .
Instead, he continued, gasoline prices are dropping for a more banal reason: "For now, it's the seasonal shift, not politics, driving the relief at the pump."
Gas prices often ease in the fall.
One reason: It's no longer summer, which is the peak season for gas. (Fewer people drive in colder weather, AAA points out .) With less demand, there's a touch more gas on the market.
Refineries also finish their annual maintenance by late fall. So that adds a bit more gas to go around.
And the blend of gasoline that's on the market gets cheaper.
Refineries make two types of gasoline every year: summer and winter blends. The summer blend produces less smog, because it evaporates less quickly in the heat; the winter blend helps engines start up in freezing weather, and uses a bit more butane, which helps lower its cost.
(Normally, the switch happens around September 15. This year, the Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of Energy said the switch would happen on September 1, citing gasoline prices that have been driven up by the war in Iran.)
But none of those are the biggest reason why gas prices are falling, says Jorge León, head of geopolitics at the research group Rystad Energy. The main driver is the falling price of Brent crude oil, which is now down to about $90 a barrel, and which is what refineries need to make gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.
That price is falling because there's a bit more oil coming out of the Middle East via pipelines, and because market traders have rejoiced at the intensifying diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran.
That progress could easily be reversed if the war escalates, León wrote in an email to NPR. "President Trump may see further military action as a way to regain negotiating leverage before Democrats take control of Congress in January. If we see renewed escalation, much of last week's oil price decline could quickly reverse," he wrote. The same would be true for gas prices.
Congressional Democrats have expressed their support for ending the war in Iran. While they have limited power to do that, they do control the power of the purse, and can withhold additional war funding or hold back confirmations of key officials.
For now, if the price of Brent crude keeps falling, so could prices at the pump. "However, this does not mean a complete 'normalization,' a return to the price levels we had before this conflict started," Jaime Brito, executive director of refining and oil markets for Dow Jones Energy, wrote in an email to NPR.
To get back to pre-Iran war gas prices, the whole oil supply chain would have to recover. Ships that have been running long alternative routes to avoid the Strait of Hormuz would have to return to their points of origin, then resume their normal routes, taking crude oil to refineries. Those refineries would have to pump out enough fuel to alleviate global demand — and depleted stockpiles. The whole process could take months after a lasting peace deal.
"Coming back to those levels will require a return to normal crude production, shipping and refining of the entire global supply chain," Brito continued.
And while $4 a gallon may seem like a bargain these days, in an update on its website, AAA said that gasoline prices are still the highest they've ever been at this time of year.

articles.title_orig: What’s the Falklands oil project at the heart of latest UK-Argentina spat?
articles.title_zh: What’s the Falklands oil project at the heart of latest UK-Argentina spat?
articles.content_orig:
The United Kingdom has pledged to defend its interests in the Sea Lion project to develop an oilfield near the Falkland Islands, as Argentina has brought a legal challenge before a tribunal over the offshore oil exploration, citing environmental concerns.
Attorney General Ellie Reeves, representing the UK government at the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS), said billions of pounds that are crucial to the future of the Falkland Islands will be lost if Argentina is successful in getting the project blocked.
The Hamburg-based tribunal is sitting for two days as Argentina seeks a provisional ruling to suspend oil drilling.
Reeves also said Argentina’s objection to the development was rooted in its territorial claims. “The hearing is not about the sovereignty of the Falklands,” the UK prime minister’s official spokesman said on Monday, echoing his country’s position that the islands’ sovereignty is not up for negotiation.
The dispute is the latest in rising tensions between the UK and Argentina over the British overseas territory in the South Atlantic Ocean.
As Vicky Kapogianni, associate professor of international and environmental law at the University of Reading, explained to Al Jazeera: “Sovereignty is the root of the dispute. The oil is the trigger, and the environment is Argentina’s best legal route.”
The Sea Lion development is a UK-Israeli venture to drill for oil in waters administered by the Falklands.
The UK’s Rockhopper Exploration and Israel’s Navitas Petroleum, operator of the Sea Lion oilfield, located about 220km (137 miles) from the islands, are expected to start the project in March 2027, with oil production to begin in 2028.
According to Rockhopper Exploration, the Sea Lion oilfield holds an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil in place, of which 500 million barrels are recoverable resources.
However, Argentina’s President Javier Milei announced measures to block the development in September and said in a post on X that he had instructed the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the country’s legal teams to initiate arbitration proceedings against the UK.
“If in 2 weeks the United Kingdom does not halt the illegitimate exploitation, we will go to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. THE MALVINAS ARE ARGENTINA’s, and they are defended with facts, not words,” he wrote, using the Argentinian name for the Falkland Islands.
Argentina formally filed a complaint at the tribunal seeking provisional measures against the UK on October 13.
The UK has administered the Falkland Islands since 1833. However, as the territory lies off Argentina’s shores, Buenos Aires claims sovereignty over what it calls Las Malvinas.
Milei has also threatened tougher sanctions on companies involved in the oil exploration project, preventing them from operating in Argentina’s oil and mining sectors.
Milei’s government argues the project violates a United Nations resolution calling on both sides to refrain from unilateral actions in the islands until their dispute over the territory’s sovereignty is resolved.
But Jorge Emilio Nunez, a reader in legal philosophy at Manchester Metropolitan University, explained that at the core of the proceedings lies the sovereignty question over the Falklands.
“The oil project is the current trigger, but it sits on top of deeper competing claims about title, the self-determination of the islanders, and control of the surrounding maritime spaces and resources,” Nunez told Al Jazeera.
“This is not only a legal dispute. It also involves domestic politics and leaders’ prestige on both sides. When valuable natural resources become commercially viable, the underlying territorial disagreement is reactivated and reframed through legal, environmental and economic arguments. The resource issue does not replace the sovereignty dispute; it intensifies it.”
On Tuesday, Attorney General Reeves told the Law of the Sea Tribunal, which issues legally binding rulings on maritime disputes, that Argentina wanted to “take control of those resources for itself”.
“The provisional measures sought by Argentina would prevent the people of the Falkland Islands from developing their natural resources as they are entitled to do so, pursuant to their fundamental right to self-determination,” she said, according to The Guardian.
“The measures sought would have devastating consequences for the Falklands people. They risk losing billions of pounds in money, which is essential for the islands’ economic development.”
But Argentina’s lawyer, Mario Oyarzabal, argued that action was needed to block the project.
“[Argentina] respects the interests of the inhabitants of the islands and their way of life as enshrined in the Argentine constitution … What these British citizens do not have is a right to decide to which state the islands belong,” he said during the hearing, The Guardian reported.
“These resources belong to the Argentine people. Some 46 million of them, including the 1,247 inhabitants born on the islands, whose interests will be duly taken into account,” he added.
In 2013, Falkland islanders voted overwhelmingly to remain with the United Kingdom, despite Argentina’s claims.
University of Reading’s Kapogianni explained that environmental risks are central issues.
“If there is a spill, oil could reach waters of Argentina’s mainland, which nobody disputes are Argentine. So the real questions are: Has the UK properly assessed that risk? Has it shared what it found? Is it ready to plan with Argentina in case of an accident?” Kapogianni told Al Jazeera.
“These are questions that can be decided without deciding who owns the islands. But where Argentina is weaker is when it asks to protect the environment in the waters around the islands themselves, the disputed waters. This is where the problem begins, because it can be assumed that those waters are Argentina’s to protect, which takes us back to the question of sovereignty.
“So yes, in that way, meaning indirectly and through the questions, sovereignty is at the heart of it. But it’s not the question the tribunal can answer. The environment is,” she said.
On Monday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s official spokesperson told the Independent news outlet that the UK was “fully engaged in the UNCLOS [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] process, and we’ll clearly set out our position on Argentina’s request for provisional measures before the Tribunal”.
“We’ll continue to robustly defend our interests and those of the Falkland Islanders,” the spokesperson added.
Last month, Burnham also discussed the bid to block the oil project during a call with United States President Donald Trump .
“The prime minister raised the economic consequences of Argentina’s coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources,” Burnham’s office said.
The fraught relationship between the UK and Argentina remains tense and heavily focused on the Falkland Islands.
Milei has capitalised on Trump’s refusal to say whether Washington would support the UK in a future conflict over the Falklands after the US president criticised London for not doing more to support the US during its attacks on Iran.
In September, Milei said the “winds of change” were blowing in Argentina’s favour when it comes to its claims of sovereignty.
“The United States is considering this change in position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come,” Milei said.
At the same time, Argentina is set for an election next year, when the Sea Lion project’s halt could help Milei’s polling position.
To Nunez, the tribunal could have a “modest domestic impact” in the country.
“A visible legal success would allow the government to claim it is actively defending national interests and resources as the Falklands/Malvinas issue carries strong symbolic wei

articles.title_orig: Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
articles.title_zh: Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
articles.content_orig:
Joe is based in Brussels, where he focuses on European politics and defence. He has covered the Ukraine war and its peace negotiations and reported on US elections from Washington DC
Britain and France should immediately deploy troops to Ukraine, a former head of Nato has said.
Anders Fogh Rasmussen accused Europe’s two nuclear powers of presiding over a “coalition of the waiting” while the Kremlin dragged out peace talks.
“For some months, France and the UK have tried to establish a coalition of the willing, but it’s more now a coalition of the waiting,” the 73-year-old former Danish prime minister told The Telegraph from his office in Brussels.
“We should transform that into a ‘coalition of the doing’ by deploying troops… you could not wait for a peace deal but actually push for peace by telling Putin ‘you cannot deter us, and we will help the Ukrainians defend against attacks against their critical infrastructure’.”
Mr Rasmussen’s call for action came during US-led negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine and Russia, which focused on security guarantees and preventing a future war.
European officials were kept out of the room after Moscow objected to their involvement in the two-day talks, which Ukraine described on Wednesday as “one of the toughest” negotiations yet.
Vladimir Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, said after the talks: “We have no idea what the Europeans are doing here, this is a trilateral meeting. They can hang out in the lobby if they want.”
Mr Rasmussen, who was Nato’s secretary-general between 2009 and 2014, believes that Europe must show Vladimir Putin that it is serious in its support for Ukraine, even as it continues to be denied a seat at the table.
He has devised a five-point strategy to stop the war and prevent Europe from “sleepwalking into a permanent war on the Continent”.
He called on Germany, Spain and Greece to empty their stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to help Kyiv protect itself against Russian ballistic missile attacks, and suggested Nato extends its integrated air and missile defence systems over western Ukraine to bolster defences.
On top of this, Mr Rasmussen said the EU should confiscate more than €200bn (£175bn) in frozen Russian assets and use them to top up Kyiv’s defence budget. The “Coalition of the Willing” should be overhauled to include only countries willing to go to war with Russia should it attack Ukraine after any ceasefire is negotiated, he added.
“President Trump has chosen Moscow and sided with Vladimir Putin,” Mr Rasmussen said. “So in Europe, we have a particular responsibility for helping Ukraine, and that’s why I call on European leaders to wake up.”
He added: “It’s clear that the Russians do not want peace. Putin has no incentives to engage in the peace negotiations as long as he believes he can succeed on the battlefield.
“So, we need to change his calculus, we need to put more pressure on Russia.”
His plan would involve French and British troops as a “reassurance force” to protect Ukraine’s population centres.
It would also free up more Ukrainian resources to commit to the front line with Russia.
Mr Rasmussen insisted that such a deployment would be in line with international rules as long as it was requested by Kyiv.
However, Mr Rasmussen’s ideas are likely to be controversial amongst Europe’s Nato allies.
Numerous countries have said they would not actively shoot down Russian missiles over Ukrainian territory for fear of becoming a genuine party to the conflict.
Belgium has repeatedly blocked EU discussions about using a tranche of frozen Russian assets to fund Ukraine’s defence.
While Germany has recently warned that it cannot donate any more Patriot interceptor missiles because it doesn’t have the stockpiles to defend its own country.
“Maybe Poland is in a different situation, but Germany, I don’t understand why they cannot deliver those Patriot systems. Deliver them now; they are needed right now in Ukraine… Germany is not threatened now,” Mr Rasmussen said.
The former Nato chief, who was involved in talks with Russia when it first invaded Ukraine’s Crimea peninsula in 2014, said the Continent was right to reopen communication channels with Moscow.
But he warned against linking discussions on a ceasefire in Ukraine to negotiations over a future European security architecture, arguing that Putin would seek to exploit the talks to restrict the military capabilities of both Kyiv and the alliance.
That said, Mr Rasmussen believes Nato could ultimately offer Russia security guarantees, given that its allies have no plans to attack Moscow.
“Why not? It wouldn’t cost anything to give such a security guarantee,” he concluded.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Inside Bessent's Situation Room confrontation with Lutnick over China chip security
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Inside Bessent's Situation Room confrontation with Lutnick over China chip security
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent challenged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to label Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat in a Situation Room confrontation last week that illustrates the tension inside the Trump administration over Chinese access to Nvidia’s advanced chips, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
Trump officials have long harbored concerns that Megaspeed has circumvented US law and funneled advanced chips into China — a prospect that Treasury staffers argued should land it on Commerce’s so-called entity list of China-connected companies that could pose national security risks. But the issue gathered newfound attention and importance in recent days when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a Megaspeed employee suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Senior Trump officials, including Lutnick, also were briefed months ago about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who the intelligence community suspected of being a Chinese spy, people familiar with the matter said.
But despite those warnings, Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list, the people said.
Confronted on it by Bessent last Thursday, Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action, they said.
Axios first reported the Situation Room confrontation.
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company that was originally incorporated in 2015 as a Chinese video game developer called 7Road International. But in the three years since Alice Huang became director and the company changed its name, it has become one of the largest buyers of Nvidia chips in Asia , purchasing more than $4 billion worth of its semiconductors, by some analyst estimates.
Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and said it is a “compliant and legal company.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy “groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.”
The entity list represents one of the US’s most significant tools for preventing American firms from selling their products to foreign companies and organizations. But adding Megaspeed to the list could also risk inflaming tensions with China amid Trump’s efforts to manage the US’ trade relationship with the fellow superpower. The Commerce Department hasn’t added any company to the list in more than a year.
Representatives for the Treasury and Commerce departments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: NASA takes an all-hands-on-deck approach in its return to the Moon
articles.title_zh: NASA takes an all-hands-on-deck approach in its return to the Moon
articles.content_orig:
Senior NASA officials held a lengthy news conference last weekend, laying out a series of lunar contract awards, new contract opportunities, and mission decisions. They followed one after the other: landers, nuclear-powered rovers, scouting drones, power generation, storage, and communication satellites.
“Hopefully, we’re keeping industry on their toes trying to catch up to all the solicitations we’re doing,” said Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program, more than 90 minutes into the news conference. “This is what it takes to do the Moon Base in the timeline we have set forth.”
The rapid-fire announcement of awards tells us a few things about NASA’s efforts to return to the Moon and establish a durable settlement there during the next decade.
First, the agency is serious about this effort—the Artemis Moon Base program represents the most credible effort to establish a permanent outpost on another world in NASA’s history. Second, NASA is reaching out to all corners of the US commercial space industry, casting an extraordinarily wide net to reach companies that have yet to fly any hardware into orbit. Third, NASA is getting creative about how it’s buying these services, and this may matter most of all.
There was a lot packed into the announcements this weekend, so to make sense of it all, I called Mike Gold, a lawyer and former NASA associate administrator who set up the Artemis Accords, who is now the president of Redwire Space. He was at NASA at the beginning of Artemis and understands what it takes to get the government moving. He said he was blown away. During a period of seven days, Gold said, NASA put out five proposals for lunar contracts.
“The pace that’s occurring, and the nature of the procurements is unprecedented,” Gold said. “You are seeing an all-hands-on-deck approach. Big companies, small companies, new companies, old companies.”
What has impressed Gold most about NASA’s strategy since announcing the Moon Base in March, at the Ignition event , has been the agency’s evolving procurement strategy. The space agency has adopted a flexible procurement strategy similar to one used by the US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.
There are two components. NASA has largely used a mechanism called Broad Agency Announcements, which ask for a capability such as providing power on the surface of the Moon. This allows NASA to ask industry for ideas without being too prescriptive and levying a bunch of requirements. It’s rather like instead of telling industry precisely what it wants, NASA asks industry what it can do.
Critically, Gold said, the space agency has also used a DARPA-style preliminary proposal process. In response to a traditional procurement, interested companies would prepare a detailed proposal, often running dozens, if not hundreds, of pages. This required an extraordinary amount of time.
With the Moon Base, NASA is employing a two-step process. After NASA announces the need for a service, interested companies submit a short white paper describing their solution. After a short review, NASA identifies the concepts it wants to pursue further, and only then do companies invest the time and resources to prepare a detailed proposal.
Gold said several lunar opportunities interested Redwire, and the company submitted initial proposals in response. But it only had to prepare a full proposal for opportunities that NASA wanted to pursue, including using a variant of its roll-out solar arrays on the Moon to generate power.
“We were able to focus the lion’s share of our resources in what the agency really wanted and what we were best at,” he said.
From this shift, it seems clear that NASA is trying to move away from micromanaging every individual lunar-base subsystem and instead seeks to coordinate independently developed commercial capabilities. The space agency is sourcing them from everywhere, from major contractors like Lockheed Martin, SpaceX, Blue Origin, and Northrop Grumman to relatively new startups such as Impulse Space, ispace-US, Voyager Technologies, Quantum Space, and more.
With questions emerging about how committed SpaceX is to NASA work in the future, the space agency appears to be seeking to diversify the way it gets cargo to the Moon. For example, it is leaning into Relativity Space and its large (but unproven) Terran R rocket, as well as orbital transfer vehicles built by Impulse Space. NASA is prioritizing the creation of a whole ecosystem of potential contractors rather than relying on one or two primes.
In doing so, NASA is taking a big risk. It is attempting to accelerate its lunar program by buying services from companies whose hardware is not yet operational and, in some cases, exists only as advanced engineering designs. For NASA, ultimately, it is a high-risk, high-reward approach. But in a demanding contest with China to reach and establish settlements on the Moon, NASA’s post-Apollo timidity is no longer tenable.
So how will NASA pay for all of the new stuff? Some of the funding is being repurposed from the previously shuttered Lunar Gateway program, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said. For example, as part of the “One Big Beautiful Bill” act passed in 2025, NASA received $2.6 billion for the Gateway. Some of the funding was already appropriated through the agency’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services Program.
Moreover, Isaacman said, some of these contracts are relatively small and will enable NASA to invest more down the road in successful services.
“By doing a lot of littles, and learning from our approach and also putting some good wins on the board, we’re demonstrating that we can be very efficient and responsible with taxpayer dollars,” he said. With this approach, he added, “You give future administrations the option of how they can dial up or down missions. Some of these missions in the, call it, $200 million range between launch, lander, and payload; potentially, you can add those or drop those inside a $25 billion approximate budget per year without putting the entire program at risk.”

articles.title_orig: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31
articles.title_zh: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31
articles.content_orig:
Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms
Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.
Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.
She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later.
“It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”
Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.
“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.
“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”
The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, blamed a deceitful fossil fuel industry and countries that “keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C”. His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.
“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”
Guterres said oil and gas companies had distorted science and delayed action on the climate crisis, and called for a windfall tax on their bumper profits they have made from the Iran war. “It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said, to applause. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”
Unusually, Turkey is co-hosting Cop with Australia, with the leaders of both countries, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Anthony Albanese respectively, each praising the partnership.
Erdoğan said he wants Cop31 to be remembered as a turning point in the climate crisis and called on countries to act, rather than just make promises. “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” the Turkish president said. However, on Monday, away from the conference hall, ​​Erdoğan celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields with an estimated in-situ potential of 135m barrels.
In her speech before world leaders, Heine said every new oil well drilled and every piece of coal extracted was a threat to her country’s future. Without naming any individual oil or gas producer, she added: “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate but something to fear.”
Albanese said the conference was a “historic moment” for Australia. The country is one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and liquified gas. Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on the climate crisis, but he was criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech.
The gathering of leaders was relatively threadbare. While 91 national leaders attended, according to the UN, major figures such as Donald Trump of the US and Xi Jinping of China were absent. Perhaps tellingly, some other leaders who declined to attend, including the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, are instead heading to Ireland for a conference on AI.
Almost every country at Cop31 is lagging in cutting emissions, with insufficient finance for the nations most vulnerable to extreme heat, floods, fires and other climate-fuelled calamities.
Although the world is barrelling past the 1.5C limit and is entering the teeth of one of the strongest El Niño events in history , there is little sign that the talks will feature any further progress on phasing out planet-heating fossil fuels.
“I’m getting a feeling of panic from around here, from the science community,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics, who described fraught conversations with rainforest and cryosphere scientists. “The mood is gradually darkening among scientists. In fact, people talk about feeling as though things have gone backwards.”
Small island nations face an existential threat from rising sea levels and are some of the countries most exposed to catastrophe when global heating shoots past 1.5C. The UN Environment Programme has found that such overshoot is now inevitable, and warned that its effects on icy regions will be so calamitous it should be kept as brief and low as possible.
Other world leaders stressed the urgency of this moment of multiple crises and the need for multilateralism to finally deliver. Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, the president of North Macedonia, said: “We are the first generation to fully understand the consequences of our choices – and perhaps the last with time to change course. Future generations will live with the consequences of our decisions.”

articles.title_orig: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
articles.title_zh: Poundland set for more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
articles.content_orig:
Poundland and its 11,000 employees are hopeful that the retailer's impending collapse can be delayed to allow time for a last-minute rescue deal.
The discount chain has been edging towards administration after being blocked by its owners from accessing cash in its bank accounts.
A deadline to secure a buyer for the business is set to expire at midnight, but sources close to the situation have told the BBC that they expect more time will be given, thanks to the release of £10m in funding.
A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers, Poundland's US owners, on Wednesday following accusations that the investment firm hopes to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 stores and stock piecemeal.
Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock stores and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.
The investment firm has denied the claims.
But pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.
However, sources close to the matter told the BBC on Tuesday that a release of £10m by its owners, while "small in the scale of things" could help at least postpone the chain's collapse while a longer term solution was explored.
Following the behind-closed-doors meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chair Liam Byrne said he was "deeply concerned" that firm's behaviour "may have jeopardised thousands of jobs on Britain's high streets".
"Over the last 17 months, they have taken millions out of Poundland when the business was on a 'knife edge'," he posted on social media.
"Now Poundland appears to be on the rebound, there's concerning signs it's been strangled of access to its own funds in what should be its busiest trading period in the run up to Christmas."
He claimed that Gordon Brothers refused to say it would prioritise saving jobs "over and above its own financial returns", but added the prospect of a good outcome for the business was "now higher thanks to the focus on the business of the last week".
He called on Gordon Brothers "to do the right thing" and give Poundland access to its own funds and work to protect the maximum number of jobs.
The 10-day moratorium to protect Poundland from its creditors expires on Thursday, but if there is a prospect of a solvent deal, the deadline could be extended.
Views on the chain's performance differ between those running operations and the owners.
Poundland boss Barry Williams told staff last week that like-for-like sales, which exclude new store openings, were up 11.4%. The sales period included Halloween, but Williams said this was £1.5m ahead of budget.
He added the business made a profit of £18.1m in the year to September, which was a "strong recovery" from the previous year where there were losses of £68m.
However, Gordon Brothers has painted a different picture, saying the chain remains "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".
There has been interest from the likes of Poundstretcher, Tesco and B&M in picking up Poundland stores which could mean continuing employment for workers in the event the chain is broken up and sold off in chunks.
The main issue is whether a piecemeal sale would protect more jobs than a buyer willing to keep Poundland as a national chain.

articles.title_orig: Google Voice appears to finally be working on RCS support
articles.title_zh: Google Voice appears to finally be working on RCS support
articles.content_orig:
It might finally be happening. A new Google Voice update plants seeds of RCS support, though the exact details remain unclear.
About APK Insight: In this “APK Insight” post, we’ve decompiled the latest version of an application that Google uploaded to the Play Store. When we decompile these files (called APKs, in the case of Android apps), we’re able to see various lines of code within that hint at possible future features. Keep in mind that Google may or may not ever ship these features, and our interpretation of what they are may be imperfect. We’ll try to enable those that are closer to being finished, however, to show you how they’ll look in case that they do ship. With that in mind, read on.
Google Voice is an invaluable tool for accessing one phone number across a host of different devices, but to say it’s becoming less impactful without support for RCS is a bit of an understatement. Now that virtually every Android phone and iPhone supports the new messaging experience, Google Voice is less useful both for business and consumer users.
But that seems to be changing.
Google Voice for Android version 2026.11.01.1014278023 doesn’t enable RCS, but it does, for the first time, actually hint that the functionality might be on its way. In a teardown of the app, one simple string stands out:
That points to a new send button used for RCS messages rather than SMS. Google Messages similarly changes its send button to differentiate between the two standards.
This update contains a host of other new strings around images, videos, and more, but none of them are directly tied to RCS support.
The folks over at Android Authority dug up some other tidbits about RCS including an “RCS chat preference” toggle and various RCS actions and messages. But, again, nothing is live just yet, and there’s no word on when it might arrive, if ever.
Google has been championing RCS support for over a decade now, so it’s long past due for Voice, a long-running Google product, to get on board. While the tidbits in this update don’t serve as any confirmation RCS if coming to Voice, it’s the most exciting update on the matter in years.

articles.title_orig: Vessel renewal incentive policy in China: Potential greenhouse gas reduction impact and opportunities for improvement - International Council on Clean Transportation
articles.title_zh: Vessel renewal incentive policy in China: Potential greenhouse gas reduction impact and opportunities for improvement - International Council on Clean Transportation
articles.content_orig:
November 11, 2026 | By: Zhihang Meng, Hae Jeong Cho, Yuanrong Zhou, Gabriel Hillman Alvarez, Jakob Schmidt
Maritime shipping plays a key role in China’s national freight sector, accounting for over 50% of transportation activity in 2024. Decarbonization of this sector at a rate in line with the government’s goal to achieve carbon neutrality before 2060 will require the large-scale application of ships fueled by low- and zero-carbon fuels.
China introduced policies in 2024 to promote the scrapping and renewal of old ships, which offer shipowners tiered subsidies to renew older ships before their mandatory retirement dates, with greater support for new/clean energy vessels (NCEVs). However, the policy does not specify which fuels NCEVs must use.
This paper estimates the potential impact of the retire-and-renew (RNR) policy on fleet renewal and greenhouse gas emissions in China’s coastal fleet. Using the Vessel Economic Guidance and Assessment (VEGA) model and Polaris, a shipping emissions projection model, we estimated fleet renewal and greenhouse gas emissions from 2025 to 2050 under the existing RNR policy design and two alternative scenarios.

Micron's ( MU ) valuation has reached a level where it's simply too cheap to ignore given its fundamentals, says Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider.
Schneider reiterated his $1,250 price target on the once red-hot AI momentum trade. It assumes about 70% upside from current levels.
"We also believe risk/reward is becoming more attractive for Neutral-rated Micron in light of the high probability of strong free cash flow in the coming quarters," Schneider said.
Micron is currently approaching tangible book value, Schneider noted. When a stock trades below tangible book value, investors value the company at less than the estimated value of its assets after subtracting its liabilities and intangible assets.
In a sense, the market is saying the company's physical and financial assets are worth more than the entire company's stock market value.
That seems to be bordering on an unwarranted disconnect , at least in assessing Schneider's work on the chip player.
Micron's stock is down 17% over the past month amid fears that a blue wave on Election Day could slow the build-out of AI infrastructure. That could have ramifications for orders for Micron's memory chips.
The rout has brought Micron's forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio down to an almost laughable 4.2 times, according to Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. Keep in mind Micron is coming off a quarter of strong demand amid memory chip shortages driving up prices.
The Street still expects Micron to grow earnings by at least 17% in its next fiscal year.

articles.title_orig: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
articles.title_zh: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
articles.content_orig:
Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.
Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.
However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.
Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."
"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.
Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said.
After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.
The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.
For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.
For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.
Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.
That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.
Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.
Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.
There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.
Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.
Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security.
Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said.
Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.
Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again.
"These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."

articles.title_orig: Iran attacks shipping navigation systems on Oman's Didamar island, sources say
articles.title_zh: Iran attacks shipping navigation systems on Oman's Didamar island, sources say
articles.content_orig:
By The Maritime Executive 2026-11-10 17:40:00
Uncertainty surrounds suggestions made that Iran has mounted an attack on navigational aids mounted on the Omani-owned Didamar Island, one of three islands which sit 10nm north of the tip of the Musandam peninsula, mid-channel between the Omani mainland and the median point in the Strait of Hormuz with Iran.
In peacetime, Didamar Island hosts the Hormuz Control Centre manned by the Royal Navy of Oman, which marshals marine traffic moving through the channels of the Traffic Separation Scheme - parts of which lie in Omani territorial waters. The slab of rock hosts a radio communications tower for radio relay and Channel 16 communications, a lighthouse, and a marine radar mounted on a 25m tower; these are important navigational aids for all ships transiting the Strait, and are maintained by Arabian Maritime and Navigation Aids Services (AMMAS), part of a network of buoys, lights and aids helping mariners navigate the Strait.
Reports of an attack seem to be based on two sources. In the first, a social media video taken at some range, smoke can be seen rising from Didamar Island. But it is not clear whether smoke is arising from the island itself, or from a stricken tanker behind and in the lee of the island. In support though, the Iranian Fars News Agency claimed that navigational aids had been struck on the ‘southern reefs’, supposedly because they had been aiding the ‘unauthorized’ transit of ships through the Strait.
Get the latest maritime news delivered to your inbox daily.
In contradiction of these reports, a senior Omani official told the Maritime Executive that navigational aids on Didamar Island had not been struck. Moreover, satellite imagery taken on the morning of November 10 does not show any obvious signs of damage to the lighthouse or the radio and radar masts, though damage to the masts might be difficult to pick up in the imagery of the available resolution.
Oman attempts to play a strictly neutral role in the conflict going on in the Strait. It respects the right of innocent passage through its waters, and is neither facilitating nor blocking those who wish to exercise that right of innocent passage. It is also almost continuously engaged in coming to the aid of ships which have been attacked, and in rescuing crews and wounded mariners, notwithstanding the dangers of Iranian follow-up attacks on targets which have been disabled. An Iranian attack on Didamar would therefore have been be a further grave breach of Omani sovereignty, to add to the IRGC transgressions that have taken place against ships in Omani territorial waters and against Omani port facilities in Duqm and Salalah.

Mortonson's colleagues downgraded their rating on Nvidia to Neutral today . Analyst Tristan Gerra's note was titled, "Icarus' Rise and Fall; Company Will be Fine."
Huang admitted to the affair on Sunday in an email to employees. Nvidia shares are down about 9.6% since the situation became public.
